description: Barebone's Parliament, Instrument of Government, Major-Generals and the Humble Petition.
content_html:
The Problem of Governing Without a Constitution

When Cromwell dissolved the Rump in April 1653 he was left with the same problem every English government since 1640 had faced: how to govern legitimately. He had no wish to be a military dictator, but every attempt to work with Parliament ended in frustration. Between 1653 and his death in 1658, Cromwell tried three constitutional experiments, each revealing the same fundamental contradiction: the army had the power, but power alone could not produce the godly, stable settlement he sought.

Barebone’s Parliament: July–December 1653

Rather than hold elections, Cromwell summoned a nominated assembly of 140 men selected for their godliness by the army and gathered churches. It was formally called the Nominated Parliament but quickly became known as “Barebone’s Parliament” after one of its more zealous members, Praise-God Barebone. Its initial reform programme was energetic: proposals to abolish tithes, replace common law with a simpler code, and reform the Court of Chancery. However, the more radical proposals alarmed conservative members. In December 1653 a moderate majority voted to dissolve the Parliament and hand power back to the army, before the radicals could act. The experiment had lasted five months.

Key Fact

Barebone’s Parliament (July–December 1653) was nominated rather than elected — its members chosen for godliness not constituency votes. It dissolved itself after only five months when moderate members voted to hand power back to the army, fearing radical proposals.

The Instrument of Government and the Protectorate

In December 1653 the army presented Cromwell with a written constitution: the Instrument of Government. This was England’s first and only written constitution. It made Cromwell Lord Protector — head of state with executive power, shared with a Council of State. Parliaments were to meet every three years, with a minimum of 160 days. The franchise was adjusted to exclude known Royalists.

Cromwell’s first Protectorate Parliament (1654–55) was confrontational from the start. MPs wanted to revise the Instrument, especially to increase parliamentary control over the army. Cromwell dissolved it after the minimum five-month period. A Royalist rising led by John Penruddock in 1655, though easily suppressed, gave him justification for more authoritarian measures.

After the Penruddock rising Cromwell divided England and Wales into eleven military districts, each governed by a Major-General. The Major-Generals were responsible for security (suppressing Royalism), taxation (a 10% tax on Royalist incomes), and moral reform: closing alehouses, suppressing bear-baiting and horse racing, and enforcing Sunday observance. The experiment lasted from August 1655 to January 1657, when Parliament — resenting both the militarism and the Puritan moral policing — voted to end it. The Major-Generals became a byword for Puritan interference in ordinary life.

Humble Petition and Advice 1657

In 1657 Parliament presented Cromwell with the Humble Petition and Advice. It offered him the crown of England. After weeks of deliberation — documented in his speeches, which show genuine uncertainty — Cromwell refused the kingship. His stated reason was that God had visibly “blasted” the title of king in England by executing Charles I; he could not take what providence had condemned. He accepted a revised version of the Petition in May 1657: he could nominate his successor (effectively making the Protectorate hereditary), an upper house of Parliament was restored, and his constitutional position was strengthened.

Oliver Cromwell died on 3 September 1658 — the anniversary of Dunbar and Worcester, which he had called his “fortunate day.” His son Richard Cromwell succeeded him but lacked his father’s authority and was forced to resign by the army in May 1659 after just eight months. The republic was entering its final crisis.

Key Fact

Cromwell refused the crown in 1657 because he believed God had judged and rejected the title of king in England. He accepted instead the right to nominate his successor and a restored upper house, under the Humble Petition and Advice.

The Protectorate faced a structural problem that Cromwell could never resolve: its legitimacy rested on military power, but broad civilian acceptance required a constitution most people could recognise. Every Parliament elected under the Instrument of Government immediately challenged that constitution. Cromwell relied on a small godly minority who shared his vision of a reformed church and society, but this minority could not command enough electoral support to govern without the army. The Humble Petition moved him towards hereditary monarchy in all but name, but without the deeper conservative legitimacy the Stuart crown possessed.
exam_tip_html: For questions on the Protectorate, organise your answer around the three constitutional experiments: Barebone’s Parliament, the Instrument of Government and the Major-Generals, and the Humble Petition. Show how each failed for a specific reason, and link these failures to the underlying problem of legitimacy. Don’t simply list the events; explain what each experiment reveals about the limits of Cromwell’s power.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Barebone’s Parliament (July–December 1653) was nominated rather than elected and dissolved itself after radical proposals alarmed moderates; the Instrument of Government then made Cromwell Lord Protector.
  • The Rule of the Major-Generals (1655–57) divided England into military districts with Puritan moral policing; it was ended by Parliament’s opposition.
  • Cromwell refused the crown offered by the Humble Petition (1657), died in September 1658, and was succeeded by his son Richard, who resigned in May 1659 under army pressure.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Instrument of Government of 1653.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: One accurate feature with supporting detail. Example: The Instrument of Government was England's first and only written constitution, produced by army officers in December 1653; it made Cromwell Lord Protector with executive power shared with a Council of State.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Rule of the Major-Generals 1655–1657.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: England and Wales were divided into eleven military districts each governed by a Major-General responsible for security and suppressing Royalist activity. Feature 2: The Major-Generals enforced Puritan moral reform — closing alehouses, suppressing horse racing and bear-baiting, enforcing Sunday observance — making them deeply unpopular.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Cromwell refused the crown offered by the Humble Petition and Advice in 1657.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains Cromwell's theological reasoning (God had blasted the title of king), his reliance on providentialist thinking, army opposition to kingship, and the practical constitutional provisions he accepted instead. Links these together. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple answer.

practice_questions.text: The Protectorate (1653–1658) successfully solved the problem of governing England after the Civil War. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing achievements (stability, foreign policy, religious toleration) against failures (no lasting constitutional settlement, each Parliament challenged the Instrument, Major-Generals unpopular, collapse after Cromwell's death). Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Both sides examined. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Barebone's Parliament dissolved itself in December 1653.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more reasons (radical proposals to abolish tithes and common law, moderate members alarmed, fear of social revolution, army concern about stability) with linked argument. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Rule of the Major-Generals was ended in 1657.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains parliamentary opposition (resentment of military rule, Puritan interference in daily life, 10% tax on Royalists), broad unpopularity, and Cromwell's need for parliamentary support for his foreign policy. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple.

Match each Protectorate institution to its description:
right: Offered Cromwell the crown — he refused it
Military governors of 11 districts enforcing Puritan moral reform

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Instrument of Government produced?
What did the Instrument of Government establish?
flashcard_questions.a: England's first written constitution; Cromwell as Lord Protector with Council of State
A nominated (not elected) assembly of 'godly' men, July–December 1653

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Barebone's Parliament dissolve itself?
flashcard_questions.a: Moderate members voted to end it before radicals could pass proposals abolishing tithes and reforming common law

flashcard_questions.q: How many military districts did Cromwell divide England into?
What did the Major-Generals enforce in their districts?
flashcard_questions.a: Royalist security, a 10% tax on Royalists, and Puritan moral reform (alehouses, bear-baiting, Sunday)

flashcard_questions.q: When did Parliament vote to end the Major-Generals?
What was the Humble Petition and Advice?
flashcard_questions.a: 1657 parliamentary offer of the crown to Cromwell; he refused the crown but accepted other powers

flashcard_questions.q: Who succeeded Cromwell as Lord Protector?
flashcard_questions.a: Richard Cromwell (resigned May 1659 under army pressure)

glossary_terms.definition: Assembly of 140 'godly' men nominated by army officers and gathered churches in 1653, known as Barebone's or the Nominated Parliament; it dissolved itself in December 1653 after radical proposals alarmed the moderates.
England's first and only written constitution, produced by army officers in December 1653, establishing Cromwell as Lord Protector with a Council of State and regular parliaments.
Cromwell's title as head of state under the Instrument of Government from December 1653; combining executive and some legislative power, falling short of kingship.
Senior army officers appointed by Cromwell in 1655 to govern military districts of England and Wales, enforce moral reform and prevent Royalist activity.
A parliamentary proposal of 1657 offering Cromwell the crown and greater civilian constitutional powers; Cromwell accepted most provisions but refused the kingship.
Son of Oliver Cromwell, briefly Lord Protector September 1658 to May 1659 before resigning under army pressure.

hero_image_caption: Cromwell as Lord Protector attempted to govern England through a series of constitutional experiments.
